Hi Olivia — thanks again for the call today. Quick recap + proposed next steps so we keep momentum: 

1) Summary of what we heard
- FastRetail is planning an initial pilot (customer support chat + product search assistance) targeting ~200K active sessions/month.
- Expected token volumes: baseline ~50M tokens/month, scale to ~200M tokens/month within 12 months (spikes during promotions).
- Budget range: $20k–$60k/month depending on SLA and throughput.

2) Caching assumptions we discussed
- Prefix caching (shared prefixes like product descriptions, common prompts) can materially reduce billed prompt tokens.
- Initial conservative prefix cache hit-rate assumption: 30–45% for retail search/chat mixes; aggressive reuse scenarios can reach 50%+.

3) Ballpark unit economics (illustrative)
- Raw model price (example): $1,800 per 1M tokens (list for the selected LLM variant in our catalog).
- Effective tokens billed = generation_tokens + prompt_tokens * (1 - cache_hit_rate).
- Example (40% hit): if you send 1M prompt tokens + 1M generation tokens, billed tokens = 1M (generation) + 1M * (1 - 0.4) = 1.6M billed. At $1,800/1M, effective cost ≈ $2,880 per 1M effective billed tokens scaled.
- Translating to an effective $/1M tokens (normalized): with a 40% prefix hit, effective $/1M ≈ $1,080 (i.e., 1,800 * (1.6 / 1.0)). With a 30% hit, ~$1,260; with 50% hit, ~$900.

4) Next steps I propose
- I attached a short pricing scenarios sheet (Pricing_Scenarios_FastRetail.xlsx) — I filled in the three hit-rate scenarios we discussed. Please confirm which baseline (50M vs 200M tokens/mo) you want modelled.
- If you can share a 2-week token sample (anonymized) or tell us a typical turn structure (prompt vs generation ratio), we’ll run a quick sample analysis and give a recommended target $/1M that maps to your budget.
- Internal: Aditya, Marcus — please see the cache notes + experimental approach below and flag any technical caveats.

Happy to jump on a 30-min follow-up to walk the spreadsheet through.

Great questions — answering inline below and adding a simple worked example so procurement can see the delta: 

Q: Per-session personalization and effect on hit rate
A: Per-session personalization can reduce cross-user prefix reuse (i.e., lower shared cache hits). That said, many prefixes are still common across users: onboarding prompts, standard product description blocks, error-handling scaffolding, and recommended-answer templates. We typically see higher hit rates on search autocomplete and product-description-heavy flows; personalization only affects the portion of the prompt that is unique.

Definition of cacheable prefix
- Cacheable prefix = contiguous initial tokens in the prompt that are identical across requests (after normalization). Practical rules we use: strip user-specific IDs, normalize timestamps, and collapse whitespace. We generally consider prefixes >= 16 tokens that match our cache index.

Worked example (concrete math)
- Assume monthly: prompt = 60M tokens, generation = 120M tokens (60/120 split = 35%/65% by tokens).
- If prefix cache hit rate = 40% on prompts: billed = generation (120M) + prompt * (1 - 0.4) = 120M + 36M = 156M billed tokens.
- If list price = $1,800 per 1M tokens, gross cost = 156 * 1.8 = $280,800 -> effective $/1M = $1,800 * (156/156) = roughly $1,800 normalized but more useful is the ratio vs raw tokens — normalized to the original 180M tokens, effective $/1M_raw = (280,800 / 180) = $1,560 per 1M raw tokens. 
- For procurement framing, we prefer quoting effective $/1M billed (after cache) and showing sensitivity to hit-rate. The sheet I attached includes the 30/40/50% scenarios.

If you can share the 7-day sample under NDA we can run a quick prefix reuse analysis and give an estimated hit-rate and a target effective $/1M that maps to your $25k–$50k budget.

Couple of technical notes to add to the thread that might affect our hit-rate estimates and how we model the experiment: 

- Prefix normalization: we should provide a short normalization script to FastRetail (strip PII, canonicalize IDs, lowercase, strip dates) — that will make their sample analysis meaningful and reproducible.
- Unit of reuse: we index prefixes by a rolling window (we use 32-token sliding anchors by default). Very short prompts (<8 tokens) rarely hit; long structured prefixes (product description + instructions) have highest reuse.
- Session personalization: if they include entire user history as prefix, the reused portion will be the static system prompt + a small subset of earlier turns. Recommend they send a sample and we run two models: (1) full-record normalization, (2) strip-per-user-history to estimate best-case shared reuse.
- Experiment plan: 7–14 day sample -> run prefix histogram -> compute hit-rate under our 32-token index -> return recommended target hits and an adjusted pricing scenario.

I've attached a tiny template to collect token samples (cache-analysis-template.csv) and will follow up with a small normalization script.
